callouts.body: **Executive Overview** **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** is an open standard protocol introduced by Anthropic (November 2024) that standardizes how AI applications connect with external data sources, tools, and systems. Often described as "USB-C for AI", MCP solves the M×N integration problem by transforming it into M+N—enabling any AI client to work with any compatible server through a universal protocol rather than requiring custom integrations for each pairing.

callouts.title: Untitled

**Navigation Guide**
This reference is organized into progressive sections: foundational concepts → technical architecture → practical implementation (Claude Code, Gemini) → PKB/Prompt Engineering applications → security → custom development. Use the Table of Contents for targeted navigation. Wiki-links connect to related PKB concepts. Callouts highlight definitions, warnings, and key claims throughout.

callouts.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
callouts.body: **Model Context Protocol** is a universal interface specification enabling bidirectional communication between AI applications (hosts) and external services (servers). It abstracts away integration complexity, allowing developers to write tools once and have them work across multiple AI platforms—Claude Desktop, Claude Code, VS Code extensions, custom agents, and more.

callouts.title: Foundation & Governance
callouts.body: %%evidence: consensus%% MCP was open-sourced by Anthropic in November 2024 and subsequently donated to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation (December 2025). The foundation includes governance participation from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, AWS, Cloudflare, and Bloomberg—signaling industry-wide adoption of this standard.

callouts.title: The Integration Problem Solved
callouts.body:
**Before MCP:**
- Claude Desktop + GitHub = Custom integration #1
- Claude Desktop + Slack = Custom integration #2
- Cursor + GitHub = Custom integration #3 (different code!)
- Each pair requires unique implementation, testing, maintenance

**After MCP:**
- GitHub MCP Server (built once)
- Slack MCP Server (built once)
- Any MCP client (Claude, Cursor, custom agents) connects to any server
- N servers + M clients = N+M components (not N×M)

callouts.title: Client-Server Architecture
callouts.body: MCP follows a client-server architecture where an MCP Host (an AI application like [[Claude Code]] or [[Claude Desktop]]) establishes connections to one or more MCP Servers through MCP Clients (connection managers).

callouts.title: Transport Mechanisms
callouts.body: MCP supports two primary transport protocols, each suited to different deployment scenarios:

callouts.title: Data Layer Components
callouts.body:
- **Lifecycle Management**: Connection initialization, capability negotiation, termination
- **Server Features**: Tools, resources, prompts exposed to clients
- **Client Features**: Sampling from host LLM, user input elicitation, logging
- **Utility Features**: Notifications for real-time updates, progress tracking

callouts.title: Tools
callouts.body: **Tools** are executable functions that the AI can invoke to perform actions with side effects. The LLM decides when to use tools based on user requests and context.

callouts.title: Tool Use Cases
callouts.body: - File operations: Create, read, update, delete files - API calls: Weather queries, database operations - System commands: Git operations, shell execution - Service integrations: Send emails, create tickets, post messages

callouts.title: Resources
callouts.body: **Resources** are data sources providing contextual information without side effects. The client application decides when and how to use resources—not the LLM.

callouts.title: Resources vs Tools
callouts.body: %%confidence: verified%% The critical distinction: Tools perform actions (side effects), while Resources provide data (read-only). Resources support real-time updates via `notifications/resources/list_changed` and `resources/subscribe`.

callouts.title: Prompts
callouts.body: **Prompts** are reusable templates for LLM interactions with parameterized messages and autocomplete support. The user triggers prompt execution, typically through slash commands.

callouts.title: Adding MCP Servers via CLI
callouts.body:
```bash
# Add server with user scope (persists across projects)
claude mcp add github --scope user

# Add with environment variables
claude mcp add digitalocean-mcp-local \
  -e DIGITALOCEAN_API_TOKEN=YOUR_TOKEN \
  -- npx "@digitalocean/mcp"

# Add HTTP/SSE server (remote)
claude mcp add --transport http notion https://mcp.notion.com/mcp

# List all configured servers
claude mcp list

# Test server connectivity
claude mcp get [server-name]

# Remove a server
claude mcp remove [server-name]
```

callouts.title: Platform Limitation
callouts.body: Gemini Code Assist MCP support is currently limited to VS Code. IntelliJ integration is not available. Android Studio has separate MCP configuration through Settings → Tools → Gemini → MCP Servers.

callouts.title: Manual Configuration Required
callouts.body: Unlike Claude Code, Gemini Code Assist cannot configure MCP servers through command palette—direct JSON editing is required.

callouts.title: Using MCP Servers in Gemini
callouts.body: 1. Open Gemini panel in VS Code 2. Select the **Agent** tab (not Chat) 3. Describe your task—agent automatically discovers and uses configured MCP servers 4. Review proposed changes before approval ⚠️ Caution: Auto-approve mode executes changes without confirmation. Use sparingly.

callouts.title: Critical Security Notice
callouts.body: MCP servers introduce significant security attack surfaces. The protocol itself does not enforce security—implementations must actively protect against threats.

callouts.title: MCPTox Research Finding
callouts.body: %%evidence: single-study%% Security research shows tool poisoning is alarmingly common in MCP ecosystems. "Rug pull" scenarios occur when legitimate tools are updated with malicious content post-approval.

callouts.title: CVE-2025-6514
callouts.body: %%evidence: single-study%% Research found 43% of analyzed MCP servers had command injection flaws—unescaped input in tools with execution capabilities, particularly dangerous with direct user input.

callouts.title: Blast Radius Concern
callouts.body: Broad scopes granted upfront (`files:*`, `db:*`, `admin:*`) expand the blast radius from compromised tokens and complicate revocation.

callouts.title: Authentication & Authorization
callouts.body: - Use OAuth with incremental scope elevation - Start with minimal scopes (`mcp:tools-basic`) - Implement WWW-Authenticate challenges for privileged operations - Use secure, non-deterministic session IDs (UUIDs with secure RNG) - Never use sessions for authentication

callouts.title: Input Validation
callouts.body:
- Sanitize all user inputs before processing
- Validate against expected schemas
- Use allowlists for file paths, commands, parameters
- Redact sensitive data in logs and outputs

callouts.title: Least Privilege
callouts.body:
- Grant minimum required permissions
- Scope access to specific resources (e.g., "sales data only")
- Implement role-based access control
- Regular permission audits

callouts.title: Supply Chain Security
callouts.body:
- Pull servers from curated sources (MCP Catalog, official repos)
- Require signature verification
- Pin versions/digests to immutable references
- Implement SAST (Static Application Security Testing)

callouts.title: Monitoring & Observability
callouts.body:
- End-to-end logging of all MCP requests/responses
- Alert on anomalous tool sequences
- Centralized SIEM integration
- Track scope elevation events with correlation IDs

callouts.title: Recommended Security Architecture
callouts.body:
**Containerization**: Isolate MCP servers in Docker containers
```bash
docker run --read-only --network=restricted mcp-server
```

**Network Limits**: Restrict egress, implement allowlists

**Resource Limits**: CPU, memory, execution time constraints

**Gateway/Middleware**: Policy enforcement layers (MCP Manager, Docker Gateway)
- Intercept, scan, log all requests/responses
- Verify signatures, redact secrets, restrict egress

callouts.title: STDIO Logging Critical
callouts.body: STDIO servers must NEVER write to stdout—this corrupts JSON-RPC communication. Use stderr for logging or dedicated log files.

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body: **Underlying Principles** MCP embodies a fundamental architectural principle: standardization enables ecosystem growth. Just as HTTP enabled the web and USB standardized device connectivity, MCP standardizes AI-tool interaction. The protocol's genius lies in its restraint—MCP defines *how* to communicate, not *what* to communicate. This separation of concerns allows infinite extensibility while maintaining interoperability. For knowledge workers, MCP represents a paradigm shift: AI assistants become first-class citizens in knowledge workflows, able to read, write, search, and modify knowledge artifacts directly rather than through copy-paste intermediation.

**Executive Overview**  
The **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** is an open, JSON-RPC-based protocol that enables structured context sharing between applications and AI models. Unlike language-specific protocols like LSP, MCP standardizes how AI assistants access files, project metadata, and custom data sources (e.g., prompt libraries, PKB graphs). While **no native integration exists yet for Claude Code or Gemini Code Assist**, a custom gateway can route MCP-served context into their prompts. For a cognitive science-backed PKB in Obsidian (via VS Code), MCP enables **context-aware prompting**, **AI agent synchronization**, and **versioned prompt retrieval**, forming the backbone of a **human-AI cognitive engineering stack**.

Your system:  
`Obsidian (PKB)` → `MCP (Context Layer)` → `Claude/Gemini (Reasoning Engines)` → `Feedback Loop`  
This mirrors a **distributed cognitive architecture**, where human and AI agents co-process information through a shared medium.

inline_fields.value: an open standard protocol that standardizes how AI applications connect with external data sources, tools, and systems through a client-server architecture using JSON-RPC 2.0
Built on concepts from the Language Server Protocol (LSP), which standardized IDE-to-language-server communication, MCP applies similar principles to AI-tool interactions
The AI application that coordinates and manages one or multiple MCP clients—examples include Claude Desktop, Claude Code, IDE extensions, and custom AI agents
A component that maintains a 1:1 connection to an MCP server and obtains context from that server for the host to use
A program that exposes context data (tools, resources, prompts) to MCP clients, running either locally or remotely
Standard Input/Output transport for local MCP servers—simple synchronous messaging where the host launches the server process and communicates via stdin/stdout pipes
Server-Sent Events over HTTP (Streamable HTTP) for remote MCP servers—asynchronous event-driven communication enabling many clients to connect to a single server
Tools are discovered via `tools/list` and invoked via `tools/call`—the server declares available tools with JSON schemas, and the client requests execution
Text resources (UTF-8 encoded: code, documents, API responses) and Binary resources (Base64 encoded: images, PDFs, archives)
Resources are identified by unique URIs such as `file:///path/to/doc`, `db://schema/table`, or `config://version`
Prompts are discovered via `prompts/list` and retrieved via `prompts/get` with dynamic payload generation based on parameters
Project scope (`.mcp.json`) > User scope (`--scope user`) > Plugin scope—project-specific configurations override user-level settings
Gemini CLI uses Google Cloud authentication (`gcloud auth login`)—no separate API key required for Gemini CLI integration
Malicious user inputs directly manipulating AI behavior through crafted prompts
Embedded instructions in external content (documents, web pages, emails) that execute when AI processes the content
Malicious instructions hidden in tool metadata/descriptions invisible to users but interpreted by AI
Plaintext credentials in environment variables, prompts, or tool arguments can leak via tool outputs, model completions, logs, or memory scraping

> from fastmcp import FastMCP
> 
> # Create server
> mcp = FastMCP("My Server Name")
> 
> # Add tool
> @mcp.tool()
> def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
>     """Add two numbers"""
>     return a + b
> 
> # Add static resource
> @mcp.resource("config://version")
> def get_version() -> str:
>     """Get server version"""
>     return "1.0.0"
> 
> # Add dynamic resource with template
> @mcp.resource("greeting://{name}")
> def get_greeting(name: str) -> str:
>     """Get personalized greeting"""
>     return f"Hello, {name}!"
> 
> # Add prompt
> @mcp.prompt()
> def greet_user(name: str, style: str = "friendly") -> str:
>     """Generate greeting prompt"""
>     styles = {
>         "friendly": "Please write a warm greeting",
>         "formal": "Please write a formal greeting"
>     }
>     return f"{styles.get(style, styles['friendly'])} for {name}."
> 
> # Run server
> if __name__ == "__main__":
>     mcp.run(transport="stdio")  # Local

unordered.text: **Configuration:** These extensions usually look for a `claude_desktop_config.json` file, or allow you to add servers via their settings UI.
**Workflow:** Open VS Code on your PKB folder. Use Claude Code in the terminal. Claude can now see your `few-shot-examples.json` and use the `filesystem` tool to read them before drafting a response.
**Mechanism:** These tools create an OpenAI-compatible endpoint for MCP servers. You then point Gemini's "Tool Use" or custom extensions to this local proxy.

**VS Code Tip:** Use the extension **Continue.dev**. It allows you to use Gemini (via API) as the model while using their "Context Providers" (which function similarly to MCP servers) to pull in local files.
**Mechanism:** The AI uses `filesystem` to read the JSON file, identifies the relevant section, and applies the examples automatically.
**Clients** (e.g., VS Code extensions) request context via `listResources()` and `readResource(uri)`.
**Servers** expose data sources (files, git, APIs) as resources with custom URI schemes.
